scene.testo: They asked him one question. Why us? Why not the Russians, the British, or the French? The man being questioned had built the most advanced weapon of the war. In May 1945, American officers wanted to know why he had walked into their hands.
On May 2, 1945, a young German rode a bicycle down a mountain road near the Austrian border. He was looking for American troops. He found one, and he spoke to him in careful English.

He told the private that his brother had invented the V-2 rocket and wanted to surrender. The American thought the man was out of his mind. Within days, the brother was sitting in front of American interrogators.
The brother was Wernher von Braun. The officers who questioned him wanted more than a surrender. They wanted his reasoning. Of every Allied nation, he had chosen one. They needed to know why.
To understand his answer, we have to go back to the last days of April. Von Braun and about a dozen of his senior engineers were waiting out the war in a ski hotel high in the Bavarian Alps.
They were not there by choice. An SS general named Hans Kammler had moved the rocket team south from central Germany. SS guards watched over them. And the engineers feared what those guards might do.
A rumor spread among the engineers. The SS, they believed, would shoot them before letting them fall into enemy hands. No such order has ever been found. But the men in that hotel believed it.
On May 1, the radio announced that Hitler was dead. The guards scattered and left. The next morning, the engineers decided not to wait for someone else to find them. They chose to go first.

They sent Magnus von Braun, Wernher's younger brother, because his English was the best in the group. The American who stopped him was Private First Class Frederick Schneikert of the 44th Infantry Division.

Schneikert passed the matter up to the division's counterintelligence men. They gave Magnus instructions and sent him back up the mountain. Bring the others with you. That evening, a small convoy of German cars rolled down toward American lines.
In one of the cars sat the man who had built the V-2. His left arm was in a huge cast, from a car accident a few weeks earlier. At Reutte, Austria, the rocket team gave itself up.

The prisoners were not what the soldiers expected. Von Braun was thirty-three years old, tall, cheerful, and talkative. The cast held his broken arm away from his body. Still, he smiled for the cameras.

He posed for photographs with American soldiers. He shook their hands. He asked for nothing except permission to keep working. One American who watched him that week said they had either captured the greatest scientist of the Reich, or its biggest liar.

So the Americans asked the question. Why did you surrender to us? The answer did not come from one sentence. It came in three parts, and later one member of the team put the group's reasoning into a single line.
We despise the French, he said. We are mortally afraid of the Soviets. We do not believe the British can afford us. That leaves only the Americans. Three nations ruled out, one by one.
Each reason had a basis in fact. France had spent four years under German occupation. The Soviet Union had lost millions of people to the German invasion, and the engineers expected no mercy there.
Britain had been hit by more than a thousand V-2 rockets, and it was close to bankruptcy. Only one country had the money, the factories, and the empty desert needed to keep building rockets.

When von Braun wrote for his captors, he was more careful. He called it a moral decision. Which victorious nation, he asked, should be trusted with what his team had created? He gave an answer with a Bible in it.

The team wanted to spare the world another war like the one Germany had just endured. That, he said, could only be assured by handing the weapon to a people guided by the Bible. It was a noble explanation. But it left something out.
The V-2 had been built underground, in tunnels dug into a mountain near Nordhausen called the Mittelwerk. The work was done by prisoners from the Mittelbau-Dora concentration camp.
About 60,000 prisoners passed through that camp. About 20,000 of them died. More people died building the V-2 than were killed by it. None of this appeared in the statement he gave the Americans.
Von Braun had joined the Nazi Party in 1937 and became an SS officer in 1940. He visited the tunnels. In the summer of 1944, he went to Buchenwald to select skilled prisoners to work on the rockets.
There was another story he told them. In March 1944, the Gestapo arrested him in the middle of the night. The charge was defeatism. Informants reported that he had said the war was going badly.
They also reported that he cared more about spaceflight than about building weapons. He spent two weeks in a cell at Stettin before General Walter Dornberger and Albert Speer secured his release.
To the Americans, the Gestapo story carried the meaning he wanted. He had never been just a weapons man. Now he had to prove it. The interrogators moved the team to Garmisch-Partenkirchen.
There they asked von Braun to put on paper where rockets would go next. He did not write a technical summary. He wrote a vision of the future, and he described the V-2 as only a beginning.

He wrote of multistage rockets, of rockets that could cross the Atlantic, of a satellite circling the Earth. He wrote of a manned station in orbit. From there, he said, a voyage to the Moon might one day be possible.

It was a remarkable document to come from a prisoner of war. The war against Japan was still being fought. The atomic bomb had not yet been used. Yet a German engineer in a Bavarian camp was promising the Moon.
It was also a sales pitch. The report told the Americans exactly what they would lose if they let this team walk away. And they already knew who else was looking for it.
The Red Army reached Peenemunde, the rocket center on the Baltic coast, on May 5. The underground plant at Nordhausen sat in territory that would be handed to the Soviets in July.

American officers worked fast. They shipped out parts for about one hundred V-2 rockets before the handover. Major Robert Staver tracked down fourteen tons of Peenemunde documents, hidden by the engineers in a mine, and moved them out in time.
In October 1946, the Soviets ran their own recruitment. In one night, they put more than 2,000 German specialists and their families on trains to the Soviet Union, whether they wanted to go or not.

Von Braun never had to make that trip. In September 1945 he landed in the United States under a secret military program, called Operation Overcast and later Paperclip. By early 1946, over a hundred of his team were at Fort Bliss, Texas.

Officially they were prisoners of war, and could not leave the base without an escort. In April 1946, at White Sands Proving Ground in New Mexico, they began firing V-2 rockets rebuilt from the parts shipped out of Nordhausen.

On January 31, 1958, von Braun's team launched Explorer 1, the first American satellite. Then they built the Saturn V. On July 16, 1969, Apollo 11 lifted off for the Moon, the journey he had described at Garmisch twenty-four years earlier.

The man who rode the bicycle down the mountain was never asked to explain his brother's choice. The man who built the rocket spent the rest of his life explaining it. He spoke of the Bible, of peace, of France, Britain, and the Soviet Union. He spoke very little of the tunnels at Nordhausen. In May 1945, Americans asked why he chose them. They never publicly asked him the price paid to build the rocket he brought with him.

descrizione:
In May 1945, American officers asked Wernher von Braun a simple question: why did he surrender to the United States? His answer, and the report he wrote for his captors, shaped the American space program. This documentary follows the surrender of the V-2 rocket team in Austria, the reasoning behind their choice, and the human cost of the weapon they built at Mittelbau-Dora.

Using documented history, interrogation records, and archival film, we trace von Braun's path from a Bavarian ski hotel to Fort Bliss, Texas, and from Operation Paperclip to Explorer 1 and Apollo 11. We also examine what his statement left out: the Nordhausen tunnels, the prisoners who died there, and his own record in the SS.

Watch to the end, and subscribe to WWII Testimony for more stories told through the words of the men who lived them.
